title: Terraform Modules: Inputs, Outputs, and Knowing When to Stop
summary: A dense field guide to Terraform modules — how variables and outputs form the contract, how module sources and version constraints resolve, how modules compose into real infrastructure, and how to recognize when a module has become too clever to maintain.

chapters.title: What a Module Actually Is
points: A module is any directory containing .tf files — nothing more; no manifest, no registration step
Every Terraform configuration has a root module: the directory where you run `terraform apply`
Child module = a module called by another module via a `module` block
`module "vpc" { source = "./modules/vpc" }` — `source` is the only required argument in a module block
Modules are called, not imported: each `module` block is a separate instantiation with its own inputs and its own resource addresses
Resource addresses inside a child module are prefixed: `module.vpc.aws_subnet.private[0]`
Modules do not create scope isolation for providers — providers are inherited from the caller by default
A module is a value-level abstraction, not a runtime boundary: everything flattens into one plan and one state file
Three module flavors: root, child (local), and published (registry/VCS)
Standard module structure: `main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`, `versions.tf`, `README.md`, `examples/`
`terraform init` is what downloads and links modules into `.terraform/modules/`; editing a module's source requires re-running init
`.terraform/modules/modules.json` records the resolved local path for every module call — useful for debugging "wrong version" confusion
Modules do not have their own state; there is one state per root module configuration
Anti-definition: a module is not a package, not a class, not a function with side effects you can call twice at will

chapters.title: Inputs: The `variable` Block
points: `variable "name" { type = string, description = ..., default = ... }` — a variable with no `default` is required
Setting `default = null` makes an argument optional while letting the module detect "not supplied"
Type constraints: primitives `string`/`number`/`bool`; collections `list(T)`, `set(T)`, `map(T)`; structural `object({...})`, `tuple([...])`
`any` disables type checking — convenient, and the most common source of confusing downstream errors
`optional(string, "default")` inside `object()` gives per-attribute defaults (Terraform 1.3+) instead of forcing full objects
`validation { condition = ..., error_message = ... }` catches bad input at plan time, not apply time
Multiple `validation` blocks are allowed; each reports independently, so write one rule per block for readable errors
`sensitive = true` redacts the value from plan output — but it still lands in plain text in state
`nullable = false` forbids explicitly passing null, distinct from having a default
Variables cannot reference other variables, resources, or data sources in their `default` — defaults must be literal
Precedence, lowest to highest: default → `terraform.tfvars` → `*.auto.tfvars` (alphabetical) → `-var-file` → `-var` → `TF_VAR_` env
`TF_VAR_name` env vars only apply to the root module; child modules get values only through their `module` block
Example: `variable "instance_count" { type = number, default = 1, validation { condition = var.instance_count > 0, error_message = "must be positive" } }`
Design rule: name variables for intent (`enable_public_access`) not implementation (`create_igw_and_route`)

chapters.title: Outputs: The `output` Block
points: `output "vpc_id" { value = aws_vpc.this.id }` — outputs are the module's only public return surface
Caller reads it as `module.vpc.vpc_id`; anything not declared as an output is unreachable from outside
`sensitive = true` on an output suppresses CLI display; consuming it in another output requires marking that one sensitive too
`description` on outputs feeds `terraform-docs` and registry documentation — not decoration
`depends_on` in an output forces ordering when a consumer needs a side effect that isn't in the value's dependency graph
`precondition` blocks in outputs assert invariants before the value is published
Root module outputs are printed after apply and readable via `terraform output -json` — the machine-readable seam to CI
`terraform_remote_state` data source reads another configuration's root outputs — cross-config coupling, use sparingly
Outputs are computed after apply; referencing an output in a `count` or `for_each` of the caller can force an unknown-value error
Export IDs and ARNs, not whole resource objects — whole objects leak schema and break on provider upgrades
Common mistake: outputting nothing, forcing callers to duplicate data lookups the module already did
Opposite mistake: outputting everything, which turns every internal rename into a breaking change
Output naming convention: `<resource>_<attribute>` singular, `<resource>_<attribute>s` for collections
Outputs plus variables are the module's contract — change either one and you owe consumers a major version bump

chapters.title: Sources: Where Modules Come From
points: Local path: `source = "./modules/network"` — must start with `./` or `../` or Terraform treats it as a registry address
Local modules are never downloaded and have no version argument; they version with your repo
Registry: `source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"` — the `<NAMESPACE>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>` triple
Private registry adds a hostname: `source = "app.terraform.io/acme/vpc/aws"`
Generic Git: `source = "git::https://github.com/acme/tf.git"`; SSH form `git::ssh://git@github.com/acme/tf.git`
GitHub shorthand: `source = "github.com/acme/tf-modules"` expands to the HTTPS Git source
`?ref=v1.2.0` pins a Git source to a tag, branch, or commit SHA — tags are mutable, SHAs are not
`//subdir` selects a subdirectory in the repo: `git::https://github.com/acme/tf.git//modules/vpc?ref=v1.2.0`
Other schemes: `hg::`, `s3::`, `gcs::`, plain HTTP archive URLs, and local `.zip` files
`source` must be a literal string — no variables, no interpolation, ever; init runs before evaluation
Credentials for Git sources come from the environment (SSH agent, `.netrc`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`), not from Terraform config
`terraform init -upgrade` is required to re-resolve a moved branch ref; plain `init` reuses the cached copy
`terraform get` fetches modules only; `init` fetches modules plus providers and backend
Trade-off table: local = fast iteration, no versioning; registry = versioned, discoverable, public; Git = versioned, private, no constraint operators

chapters.title: Versions and Constraints
points: `version` argument works only for registry sources — Git and local sources ignore it (Git uses `?ref=`)
Operators: `=`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `~>` (pessimistic), and comma-separated conjunctions
`~> 3.1` allows 3.2, 3.9 but not 4.0; `~> 3.1.4` allows 3.1.5 but not 3.2.0 — the last component is what floats
`>= 3.0, < 4.0` is the explicit spelling of a major-version pin; clearer than `~>` for readers
Modules have no lock file — only providers are locked in `.terraform.lock.hcl`, so loose module constraints drift silently
Consequence: pin modules exactly (`= 3.14.0` or a commit SHA) in production roots; float them in libraries
Semver contract for a module: MAJOR = removed/renamed variable or output, MINOR = new optional input, PATCH = internal fix
Adding a required variable with no default is a breaking change even though nothing was deleted
`required_version` in the `terraform` block constrains the CLI; a child module's constraint applies to the whole run
`required_providers` in a child module declares which providers it expects and their version ranges
Provider version constraints from all modules are intersected — one strict child module can block the whole upgrade
Pre-release versions (`1.0.0-rc1`) are excluded from ranges unless requested exactly
Upgrade practice: bump one module version, run `terraform plan`, read the diff, then commit the pin — never bulk-bump
Renovate/Dependabot both parse Terraform module versions, but only for registry and Git-tag sources

chapters.title: Composition: Wiring Modules Together
points: Composition means passing one module's output into another module's input: `subnet_ids = module.network.private_subnet_ids`
Terraform infers the dependency edge from the reference — no manual ordering needed
`depends_on` on a `module` block forces the whole module to wait; it is a blunt instrument and disables some parallelism
`count` on a module: `count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0` gives conditional creation; consumers must then index `module.x[0]`
`for_each` on a module creates one instance per key: `for_each = var.regions`, addressed `module.app["us-east-1"]`
Switching a module from `count` to `for_each` re-creates everything unless you write `moved` blocks
`moved { from = module.old, to = module.new }` refactors state without destroy/create — the safe rename tool
Providers pass explicitly for aliases: `providers = { aws = aws.us_west }` inside the module block
A module that declares its own `provider` block cannot be used with `count`/`for_each` and is a legacy anti-pattern
Prefer a flat root calling several focused modules over deep module nesting — three levels deep and plans become unreadable
Two composition styles: inversion of control (caller creates the VPC, passes IDs) vs encapsulation (module creates everything)
Inversion of control wins for reusable library modules; encapsulation wins for opinionated service-in-a-box modules
Data sources at the caller can decouple modules: look up the VPC by tag rather than threading its ID through four levels
Example wiring: `module "db" { source = "./modules/rds", subnet_ids = module.network.private_subnet_ids, sg_id = module.security.db_sg_id }`

chapters.title: Building Reusable Modules Well
points: One module = one logical unit of infrastructure; if you cannot name it in three words, it is two modules
Ship an `examples/` directory — it doubles as documentation and as the integration test target
Use `this` as the resource name for a module's single primary resource: `aws_vpc.this`
`locals` for derived values; never expose a local as a variable just to let callers override the derivation
Accept a `tags` map and merge it: `tags = merge(var.tags, { Name = var.name })` — never hardcode tags
Never hardcode region, account ID, or environment name inside a reusable module
Do not put backend or provider configuration in a child module — that belongs to the root
`terraform-docs` generates the input/output table from descriptions; wire it into CI so docs cannot rot
`terraform fmt -check -recursive` and `terraform validate` are the cheap gate; `tflint` and `checkov` are the next tier
Test with `terraform test` (native, `.tftest.hcl`) for plan-level assertions; Terratest for real apply/destroy in Go
Publish with a `terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>` repo name and semver Git tags — the registry requires both
Keep the required-input count low: every required variable is a decision you forced onto every caller
Provide sensible defaults for the 80% case, escape hatches for the rest, and no options for the 1% case
Deprecation path: keep the old variable, mark it deprecated in the description, coalesce it with the new one, remove at the next major

chapters.title: When a Module Is Too Clever
points: Smell: a boolean input that toggles whether whole resources exist — `create_x` flags multiply the plan's states to 2^n
Smell: nested `dynamic` blocks driven by deeply nested input objects — you reinvented the provider schema, badly
Smell: `for_each` over a map whose keys are themselves computed from other resources — unknown keys break plan
Smell: a `locals` block longer than the resources it feeds; logic-to-resource ratio above ~1:1 means the module became a program
Smell: input named `overrides` or `extra_config` of type `any` — the contract has given up
Smell: the module wraps a single resource and passes through every argument — that is a rename, not an abstraction
Cost of cleverness: every conditional is a code path nobody tested; combinations grow faster than your example directory
Rule of three: do not extract a module until the third real caller; two callers is coincidence
Prefer duplication over the wrong abstraction — copied HCL is cheap to delete, a bad module is load-bearing
Concrete beats configurable: two clear modules (`vpc_public`, `vpc_private`) often beat one with `var.topology`
The readability test: a reader who knows Terraform but not your module should predict the plan from the call site
The blast-radius test: if changing one input can destroy a database, that input should not exist
When to un-abstract: inline the module back into the root, delete the dead branches, then re-extract only what is shared
Counter-balance: too-thin modules are also a cost — a module that only sets two defaults adds indirection for no leverage

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and How They Bite
points: Interpolating into `source` — fails with "Variables not allowed"; module sources resolve before evaluation
Forgetting `terraform init` after adding or changing a module — plan errors with "Module not installed"
Trusting a mutable Git branch ref: `?ref=main` means your infra changes when someone else merges
Unpinned registry module in a root config: a minor bump silently rewrites your plan on the next CI run
Passing a whole resource object into a module and coupling to a provider schema that changes next release
Renaming a module block without a `moved` block — Terraform destroys and recreates everything under it
Wrapping a module in `count` after the fact — addresses shift from `module.x` to `module.x[0]`, forcing state moves
`sensitive = true` on a variable but the value still readable in `terraform.tfstate` and in provider debug logs
Provider config inside a reusable child module — blocks `for_each`, breaks removal, and warns on every plan
Cyclic composition: module A output feeds module B, module B output feeds module A — Terraform reports a cycle with no clear line number
Deeply nested modules producing plan output nobody reads, so nobody catches the accidental destroy
Using `terraform_remote_state` as a general database — creates hidden cross-team apply ordering
Assuming module `count = 0` cleans up cleanly — it destroys the resources; use `removed` blocks when you want state-only removal
Debug toolkit: `terraform providers`, `terraform graph`, `terraform state list`, `terraform console`, and `.terraform/modules/modules.json`

chapters.title: The Whole Picture
points: A module is a directory; its contract is variables in, outputs out, and nothing else is public
Sources decide where code comes from; versions decide when it changes — pin both in roots
`version` for registry, `?ref=` for Git, nothing for local paths
There is no module lock file — pinning is your job, not Terraform's
Composition is just references: output of one module into input of the next, with the graph inferred
`moved` blocks are the refactoring tool that makes module restructuring non-destructive
Design checklist: one purpose, few required inputs, useful outputs, real examples, generated docs, semver tags
Complexity checklist: count the booleans, count the `dynamic` blocks, measure locals-to-resources ratio, run the readability test
Rule of three before extraction; duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction
Encapsulation for opinionated app modules; inversion of control for shared library modules
The best module is boring: predictable plan, obvious inputs, no surprises at apply
When in doubt, make it concrete — you can always abstract later, but you cannot easily un-ship a bad interface
Progression to practice: write it inline, extract on the third repeat, tag it, pin it, document it, then leave it alone
Final measure of a module: how quickly a new teammate can call it correctly without reading its source
